label: Dutch national flag
summary: NIST DADS defines Dutch national flag as: Rearrange elements in an array into three groups: bottom, middle, and top. One algorithm is to have the top group grow down from the top of the array, the bottom group grow up from the bottom, and keep the middle group just above the bottom. The algorithm stores the locations just below the top group, just above the bottom, and just above the middle in three indexes. At each step, examine the element just above the middle. If it belongs to the top group, swap it with the element just below the top. If it belongs in the bottom, swap it with the element just above the bottom. If it is in the middle, leave it. summary: NIST DADS defines brute force string search as: Find a string in another string or body of text by trying each position one at a time. There are many far faster string matching algorithms. Also known as naive string search.

summary: NIST DADS defines buddy system as: A memory allocation strategy which recursively divides allocatable blocks of memory into pairs of adjacent equal-sized blocks called "buddies".

summary: NIST DADS defines Burrows-Wheeler transform as: Permute a string . Repeated substrings lead to repeated characters in the permuted string, which is easier to compress. label: busy beaver
summary: NIST DADS defines busy beaver as: (1) A Turing machine with a small number of states that halts when started with a blank tape, but writes a huge number of non-blanks or takes a huge number of steps. sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: bvtree

summary: NIST DADS defines Byzantine generals as: The problem of reaching a consensus among distributed units if some of them give misleading answers. Some traitorous generals may lie about whether they will support a particular plan and what other generals told them. Exchanging only messages, what decision making algorithm should the generals use to reach a consensus? What percentage of liars can the algorithm tolerate and still correctly determine a consensus?

summary: NIST DADS defines cellular automaton as: Usually a two-dimensional organization of simple finite state machines whose next state depends on their own state and the states of their eight closest neighbors. summary: NIST DADS defines centroid as: The center of gravity or center of mass of an object.

summary: NIST DADS defines chain as: A set with a total order .

summary: NIST DADS defines Chinese postman problem as: Find a minimum length closed walk that traverses each edge at least once. Finding an optimal solution in a graph with both directed and undirected edges is NP-complete .

summary: NIST DADS defines hashbelt as: Use a short list or array of hash tables to implement a hash table with aging to expire items. To expire items, add a new table at the head of the list and drop the oldest table, along with its contents. To find an item, search all the tables.

summary: NIST DADS defines Hausdorff distance as: A measure of the resemblance of two (fixed) sets of geometric points P and Q, defined as H(P,Q)=max{max a∈ P min b∈ Q d(a,b), max a∈ Q min b∈ P d(a,b)} where d(·,·) is the distance metric, usually the Euclidean distance .

summary: NIST DADS defines head as: The first item of a list .

summary: NIST DADS defines heapify as: Rearrange a heap to maintain the heap property , that is, the key of the root node is more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the keys of its children . If the root node's key is not more extreme, swap it with the most extreme child key, then recursively heapify that child's subtree. The child subtrees must be heaps to start.

summary: NIST DADS defines heap property as: Each node in a tree has a key which is more extreme (greater or less) than or equal to the key of its parent .

summary: NIST DADS defines height as: The maximum distance of any node from the root . If a tree has only one node (the root), the height is zero. The height of an empty tree is not defined.

summary: NIST DADS defines height-balanced binary search tree as: A height-balanced tree which is also a binary search tree . It supports membership, insert, and delete operations in time logarithmic in the number of nodes in the tree.

summary: NIST DADS defines height-balanced tree as: A tree whose subtrees differ in height by no more than one and the subtrees are height-balanced, too. An empty tree is height-balanced.

summary: NIST DADS defines heuristic as: An algorithm that usually, but not always, works or that gives nearly the right answer.

label: histogram sort
summary: NIST DADS defines histogram sort as: An efficient 3-pass refinement of a bucket sort algorithm. The first pass counts the number of items for each bucket in an auxiliary array , and then makes a running total so each auxiliary entry is the number of preceding items. The second pass puts each item in its proper bucket according to the auxiliary entry for the key of that item. The last pass sorts each bucket. Also known as interpolation sort.

label: homeomorphic
summary: NIST DADS defines homeomorphic as: Two graphs are homeomorphic if they can be made isomorphic by inserting new vertices of degree 2 into edges .

label: horizontal visibility map
summary: NIST DADS defines horizontal visibility map as: A partition of the plane into regions by drawing a horizontal straight line through each vertex p of a planar straight-line graph until it intersects an edge e of the graph or extends to infinity. The edge e is said to be horizontally visible from p.

label: hsadelta
summary: NIST DADS defines hsadelta as: An algorithm to produce a sequence of insert and copy commands (an edit script ) which creates a new version file from a reference file. To begin, hash every block of the reference file and store every hash in a hash value array . Build a suffix array and three other data structures for quick access. Beginning at the first location in the version file, hash a block and look for the longest match in the reference file. Upon a match, encode an insert back to the previous match and a copy of the match. If no match, look at the next location. At the end, encode an insert for remaining unmatched characters.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hsadelta

label: hybrid algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines hybrid algorithm as: Any algorithm composed of simpler algorithms.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: hybridAlgorithm

label: hyperedge
summary: NIST DADS defines hyperedge as: A connection between any number of vertices of a hypergraph . Formal Definition: A hyperedge is a set of vertices of a hypergraph.

label: ideal random shuffle
summary: NIST DADS defines ideal random shuffle as: A permutation algorithm, or shuffle, that has exactly the same chance of producing any permutation.

label: ideal merge
summary: NIST DADS defines ideal merge as: Merge n sorted streams into one output stream. To begin the streams are sorted by the value of the head element of each. Then the head of the first stream, which is the least since the streams were sorted, is removed and written to the output. That stream is inserted back into the list of streams according to its new head. Taking the head of the first stream and reinserting that stream is repeated until all elements have been processed. Using linear search to insert a stream into the list, the execution time is Θ(M N) where M is the total number of elements. Keeping the streams in a heap , the execution time is Θ(M log N) .

summary: NIST DADS defines internal node as: A node of a tree that has one or more child nodes, equivalently, one that is not a leaf . Also known as nonterminal node.

summary: NIST DADS defines intersection as: The intersection of two sets is a set having those members which are in both sets.

summary: NIST DADS defines intractable as: A problem for which no algorithm can exist which computes all instances of it in polynomial time .

summary: NIST DADS defines introspective sort as: A variant of quicksort which switches to heapsort for pathological inputs, that is, when execution time is becoming quadratic. Also known as introsort.

summary: NIST DADS defines inverse suffix array as: For each position in a string , the inverse suffix array has its index in the string's suffix array . Formal Definition: Given a suffix array, sa, and the corresponding inverse suffix array, isa, isa[i] = j iff sa[j] = i.

label: inversion list
summary: NIST DADS defines inversion list as: A set of non-overlapping numeric ranges, stored in an array in increasing order. Items in odd indexes begin ranges, and items in even indexes are the first number after the ends. Use a form of binary search to determine if a number is in any of the ranges. If the search ends on an odd index (a beginning), the number is in the set. If the search ends on an even index (a just-after-end) or outside the array, it is not in the set.

summary: NIST DADS defines inverted file index as: An inverted index that only indicates the text in which a word appears, not where the word appears within the text.

summary: NIST DADS defines inverted index as: An index into a set of texts of the words in the texts. The index is accessed by some search method. Each index entry gives the word and a list of texts, possibly with locations within the text, where the word occurs.

summary: NIST DADS defines invertible Bloom lookup table as: Algorithms and an array of cells to store key/value pairs. Each cell has a count of how many pairs are mapped to the cell, the sum of the keys mapped to it, and the sum of the values mapped to it. Using k hash functions , each pair is mapped to T[h 1 (k)], T[h 2 (k)], ..., T[h k (k)]. Also known as IBLT.

summary: NIST DADS defines isomorphic as: Two graphs are isomorphic if there is a one-to-one correspondence between their vertices and there is an edge between two vertices of one graph if and only if there is an edge between the two corresponding vertices in the other graph.

summary: NIST DADS defines J sort as: An in-place sort algorithm that uses strand sort to sort fewer than about 40 items and shuffle sort to sort more.

label: Jaro-Winkler
summary: NIST DADS defines Jaro-Winkler as: A measure of similarity between two strings . The Jaro measure is the weighted sum of percentage of matched characters from each file and transposed characters. Winkler increased this measure for matching initial characters, then rescaled it by a piecewise function, whose intervals and weights depend on the type of string (first name, last name, street, etc.).

label: jelly-fish
summary: NIST DADS defines jelly-fish as: A theoretical data structure for n items. It starts with a balanced binary search tree of about √(n) nodes. The leaf nodes lead to "tentacles" or linked lists , each of about √(n) nodes.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: jellyfish

label: Johnson-Trotter
summary: NIST DADS defines Johnson-Trotter as: Generate permutations by swapping one adjacent pair of elements at a time. Also known as Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter, Trotter-Johnson.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: johnsonTrotter

label: Johnson's algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines Johnson's algorithm as: An algorithm to solve the all pairs shortest path problem in a sparse weighted, directed graph . First, it adds a new node with zero weight edges from it to all other nodes, and runs the Bellman-Ford algorithm to check for negative weight cycles and find h(v), the least weight of a path from the new node to node v. Next it reweights the edges using the nodes' h(v) values. Finally for each node, it runs Dijkstra's algorithm and stores the computed least weight to other nodes, reweighted using the nodes' h(v) values, as the final weight. The time complexity is O(V²log V + VE) .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: johnsonsAlgorithm

label: k²-tree
summary: NIST DADS defines k²-tree as: A compact representation of a sparse directed graph . It requires 1 to 3 bits per edge. Many access functions, like successor(s), predecessor(s), and range (all links from a range of vertices to another range of vertices), have very efficient implementations.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: k2tree

label: Karnaugh map
summary: NIST DADS defines Karnaugh map as: A method for minimizing a boolean expression , usually aided by a rectangular map of the value of the expression for all possible input values. Input values are arranged in a Gray code . Maximal rectangular groups that cover the inputs where the expression is true give a minimum implementation. Also known as Veitch diagram, KV diagram.

label: Karp-Rabin
summary: NIST DADS defines Karp-Rabin as: A string matching algorithm that compares string's hash values, rather than the strings themselves. For efficiency, the hash value of the next position in the text is easily computed from the hash value of the current position. Also known as Rabin-Karp.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karpRabin

label: Karp reduction
summary: NIST DADS defines Karp reduction as: A reduction given by a polynomial time computable transformation function.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karpreductin

summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary Huffman coding as: A minimal variable-length coding based on the frequency of each character. Similar to a Huffman coding , but joins k trees into a k-ary tree at each step, and uses k symbols for each level.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyHuffman

summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary tree as: A tree with no more than k children for each node . Also known as k-way tree.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyTree

summary: NIST DADS defines k-ary heap as: A complete tree where every node has a key more extreme (greater or less) than the key of its parent . Each node has k or fewer children .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: karyheap

label: k-coloring
summary: NIST DADS defines k-coloring as: 1) The assignment of k colors (or any distinct marks) to the vertices of a graph . 2) The assignment of k colors to the edges of a graph . A coloring is a proper coloring if no two adjacent vertices or edges have the same color.

summary: NIST DADS defines k-connected graph as: A connected graph such that deleting any k-1 vertices (and incident edges ) results in a graph that is still connected.

summary: NIST DADS defines k-d-B-tree as: A data structure which splits multidimensional spaces like an adaptive k-d tree , but balances the resulting tree like a B-tree .

summary: NIST DADS defines k-dimensional as: (1) Dealing with or restricted to a space where location can be completely described with exactly k orthogonal axes. (2) Dealing with a space of any number of dimensions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdimensional

summary: NIST DADS defines K-dominant match as: A match [i,j] having rank k and such that for any other pair [i',j'] of rank k either i'>i and j'≤ j or i' ≤ i and j'>j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdominant

summary: NIST DADS defines k-d tree as: A multidimensional search tree for points in k dimensional space. Levels of the tree are split along successive dimensions at the points.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kdtree

label: key
summary: NIST DADS defines key as: The part of a group of data by which it is sorted, indexed, cross referenced, etc.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: key

label: knight's tour
summary: NIST DADS defines knight's tour as: A series of moves of a chess knight that visits all squares on the board exactly once.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: knightstour

label: Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines Knuth-Morris-Pratt algorithm as: A string matching algorithm that turns the search string into a finite state machine , then runs the machine with the string to be searched as the input string. Execution time is O(m+n) , where m is the length of the search string, and n is the length of the string to be searched. Also known as KMP.

summary: NIST DADS defines Kolmogorov complexity as: The minimum number of bits into which a string can be compressed without losing information. This is defined with respect to a fixed, but universal decompression scheme, given by a universal Turing machine .

summary: NIST DADS defines Kripke structure as: A nondeterministic finite state machine whose states are labeled with boolean variables, which are the evaluations of expressions in that state. It may be extended with fairness constraints.

summary: NIST DADS defines k-way merge sort as: A merge sort that sorts a data stream using repeated merges. It merges runs from the k streams into an output stream. It then repeatedly distributes the runs in the output stream to the k streams and merges them until there is a single sorted output. Also known as p-way merge sort.

summary: NIST DADS defines k-way merge as: Combine k sorted data streams into a single sorted stream.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: kwaymerge

summary: NIST DADS defines labeled graph as: A graph which has labels associated with each edge or each vertex .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: labeledgraph

summary: NIST DADS defines language as: A set of strings over some fixed alphabet . A characterization of inputs which may or may not be solved by algorithms . Also known as formal language.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: language

summary: NIST DADS defines Las Vegas algorithm as: A randomized algorithm that always produces correct results, with the only variation from one run to another being its running time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lasVegas

summary: NIST DADS defines last-in, first-out as: A policy that the most recently arrived item is processed first. A stack implements this.

summary: NIST DADS defines lattice as: A point lattice generated by taking integer linear combinations of a set of basis vectors.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lattice

summary: NIST DADS defines LCFS hashing as: In case of collision , move the existing item to another position, dictated by the open addressing scheme used.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: lcfsHashing

summary: NIST DADS defines least common multiple as: The least integer which is a multiple of given integers. For instance, LCM(6, 10) = 30. Also known as LCM.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: leastCommonMultiple

summary: NIST DADS defines leftist tree as: A priority queue implemented with a variant of a binary tree . Every node has a count which is the distance to the nearest leaf . label: omega
summary: NIST DADS defines omega as: The Greek letter written as ω (see ω(n) ) or Ω (see Ω(n) ).

summary: NIST DADS defines lexicographical order as: Alphabetical or "dictionary" order.

summary: NIST DADS defines linear hash as: A numeric function that maintains the order of input keys while changing their spacing. Formal Definition: A hash function f for keys in S such that k1, k2 ∈ S ∧ k1 > k2 → f(k1) > f(k2). Also known as order-preserving hash.

summary: NIST DADS defines linear quadtree as: A quadtree implemented as a single array of nodes .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: linearquadtr

summary: NIST DADS defines link as: A reference, pointer, or access handle to another part of the data structure. Often, a memory address.

summary: NIST DADS defines linked data signature as: A digital signature, and information to verify it, for linked data. Also known as LDS.

summary: NIST DADS defines list contraction as: Contracting a list by removing some of the items.

label: little-o notation
summary: NIST DADS defines little-o notation as: A theoretical measure of the execution of an algorithm , usually the time or memory needed, given the problem size n, which is usually the number of items. summary: NIST DADS defines local alignment as: The detection of local similarities among two or more strings .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: localitySensitiveHashing

label: local optimum
summary: NIST DADS defines local optimum as: A solution to a problem that is better than all other solutions that are slightly different, but worse than the global optimum .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: localoptimum

summary: NIST DADS defines logarithmic as: (1) Any function that is a constant times the logarithm of the argument: f(x)=c log x. (3) Sometimes imprecisely used to mean polylogarithmic .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: logarithmic

label: longest common subsequence
summary: NIST DADS defines longest common subsequence as: The problem of finding a maximum length (or maximum weight) subsequence of two or more strings . Also known as heaviest common subsequence.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: longestCommonSubsequence

label: longest common substring
summary: NIST DADS defines longest common substring as: Find the longest substring of two or more strings .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: longestCommonSubstring

summary: NIST DADS defines lower triangular matrix as: A matrix that is only defined at (i,j) when i ≥ j.

label: rescalable
summary: NIST DADS defines rescalable as: An optimization for which given any instance of the problem and integer λ >0, there is an easily computed second instance that is the same except that the objective function for the second instance is (element-wise) λ times the objective function of the first instance. sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rescalable

label: reservoir sampling
summary: NIST DADS defines reservoir sampling as: Randomly select k items from a stream of items of unknown length. Save the first k items in an array of size k. For each item j, j > k, choose a random integer M from 1 to j (inclusive). If M ≤ k, replace item M of the array with item j.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: reservoirSampling

label: restricted universe sort
summary: NIST DADS defines restricted universe sort as: A sort algorithm that operates on the basis that the keys are members of a restricted set of values. They may not require comparisons of keys to perform the sorting.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: restricted

label: R-file
summary: NIST DADS defines R-file as: A spatial access method which divides space into a hierarchically of nested boxes. Objects are indexed in the lowest cell which completely contains them.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rfile

label: ρ-approximation algorithm
summary: NIST DADS defines ρ-approximation algorithm as: An approximation algorithm guaranteed to find a solution at most (or at least, as appropriate) ρ times the optimum. The ratio ρ is the performance ratio or relative performance guarantee of the algorithm.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rhoapproxmtn

label: Rice's method
summary: NIST DADS defines Rice's method as: A method of complex asymptotics that can handle certain alternating sums arising in the analysis of algorithms.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: ricesmethod

label: right-threaded tree
summary: NIST DADS defines right-threaded tree as: A variant of a threaded tree in which only the right thread, i.e. link to the successor, of each node is maintained.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rightThreadedTree

label: right rotation
summary: NIST DADS defines right rotation as: (1) In a binary search tree , pushing a node N down and to the right to balance the tree. N's left child replaces N, and the left child's right child becomes N's left child. (2) In an array , moving all items to the next higher location. sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rightrotatn

label: Robin Hood hashing
summary: NIST DADS defines Robin Hood hashing as: In case of collision , the item with the longer probe sequence stays in the position. The other item is moved. This tends to equalize the length of probe sequences.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: robinHoodHashing

label: rooted tree
summary: NIST DADS defines rooted tree as: A tree in which one node is designated as the root . Also known as oriented tree.

label: rotation
summary: NIST DADS defines rotation as: To switch children and parents among two or three adjacent nodes to restore balance to a tree .

label: RP
summary: NIST DADS defines RP as: The class of languages for which membership can be determined in polynomial time by a probabilistic Turing machine with no false acceptances and less than half false rejections. "RP" means " R andomized P olynomial" time. Formal Definition: For a language, S, there exists a probabilistic Turing machine , M, that accepts or rejects any string in polynomial time . If w ∉ S, M rejects w. If w ∈ S, M accepts w with a probability at least 1/2. Also known as randomized polynomial time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rp

label: R-tree
summary: NIST DADS defines R-tree as: (1) A spatial access method that splits space with hierarchically nested, and possibly overlapping, boxes. The tree is height-balanced. (2) A recursion tree .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: rtree

label: run time
summary: NIST DADS defines run time as: (1) The amount of time needed to execute an algorithm . (2) The time when a compiled program is executing, versus compile time.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: runtime

label: saturated edge
summary: NIST DADS defines saturated edge as: An edge in a flow network which has the maximum possible flow.

label: SBB tree
summary: NIST DADS defines SBB tree as: A symmetric binary B-tree. Now known as a red-black tree .

label: scan
summary: NIST DADS defines scan as: A parallel operation in which each element in an array or linked list receives the sum of all previous elements. Also known as prefix sums.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: scan

label: scapegoat tree
summary: NIST DADS defines scapegoat tree as: A binary search tree that needs no balance information. Search time is logarithmic , and the amortized cost of update is logarithmic .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: scapegoatTree

label: search tree
summary: NIST DADS defines search tree as: A tree where every subtree of a node has keys less than any other subtree of the node to its right. The keys in a node are conceptually between subtrees and are greater than any keys in subtrees to its left and less than any keys in subtrees to its right.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: searchtree

label: search tree property
summary: NIST DADS defines search tree property as: When the key of every node of a binary tree is larger than the key of its left child and smaller than its right child.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: searchtrprop

label: secant search
summary: NIST DADS defines secant search as: Search a sorted array by estimating the next position to check based on the values at the two previous positions checked.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: secantSearch

label: secondary clustering
summary: NIST DADS defines secondary clustering as: The tendency for some collision resolution schemes to create long run of filled slots away from a key hash position, e.g., along the probe sequence .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: secondaryClustering

label: segment
summary: NIST DADS defines segment as: (1) The substring of a pattern delimited by two don't cares or one don't care and beginning or end of the pattern. (2) A substring .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: segment

label: Select
summary: NIST DADS defines Select as: A four-part algorithm to select the k th smallest element of an array . sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: select

label: select and partition
summary: NIST DADS defines select and partition as: Given an array A of n elements and a positive integer k ≤ n, find the k th smallest element of A and partition the array such that A[1], …, A[k-1] ≤ A[k] ≤ A[k+1], …, A[n].

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectAndPartition

label: select mode
summary: NIST DADS defines select mode as: An algorithm to find the mode, or most frequently occurring value, in a group of elements.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selectmode

label: self-organizing list
summary: NIST DADS defines self-organizing list as: A list that reorders the elements based on some self-organizing heuristic [Wikipedia] to improve average access time.

label: self-loop
summary: NIST DADS defines self-loop as: An edge of a graph which starts and ends at the same vertex .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: selfloop

label: semidefinite programming
summary: NIST DADS defines semidefinite programming as: A generalization of a linear program in which any subset of the variables may be constrained to form a semidefinite matrix.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: semidefinite

label: separate chaining
summary: NIST DADS defines separate chaining as: A scheme in which each position in the hash table has a list to handle collisions . Each position may be just a link to the list ( direct chaining ) or may be an item and a link, essentially, the head of a list. In the latter, one item is in the table, and other colliding items are in the list. Also known as external chaining.

summary: NIST DADS defines separation theorem as: A theorem showing that two complexity classes are distinct. Most separation theorems have been proved by diagonalization .

summary: NIST DADS defines set packing as: An optimization problem to find the largest number of mutually disjoint subsets that cover a given set of sets .

label: shadow heap
summary: NIST DADS defines shadow heap as: A heap , implemented in an array , adjacent to an unordered table. The shadow is the table nodes and all their (recursive) parents , by array index, in the heap.

summary: NIST DADS defines shadow merge as: An algorithm to merge two heaps by concatenating the smaller heap to the larger, then reordering just the concatenated nodes and their parents to restore the heap property.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowmerge

label: shadow merge insert
summary: NIST DADS defines shadow merge insert as: An algorithm to insert a new node into a shadow heap . The new node is placed in the unordered table. When the table grows beyond some threshold size, table nodes and all their parents are reordered so everything is a heap.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shadowmrgins

label: Shannon-Fano coding
summary: NIST DADS defines Shannon-Fano coding as: A variable-length coding based on the frequency of occurrence of each character. Divide the characters into two sets with the frequency of each set as close to half as possible, and assign the sets either 0 or 1 coding. Repeatedly divide the sets until each character has a unique coding.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shannonFano

label: shared memory
summary: NIST DADS defines shared memory as: All processors have the same global image of (and access to) all of the memory.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sharedmemory

label: Shift-Or
summary: NIST DADS defines Shift-Or as: A string matching algorithm which keeps an array of bits, R, showing if prefixes of the pattern don't match at the current place. Before searching, mismatch arrays are computed for each character in the alphabet and saved in an array, S. For the next position, with the character c, R = shift(R) or S[c]. If the last bit of R is 0, the pattern matches.

label: shortest common supersequence
summary: NIST DADS defines shortest common supersequence as: Find the shortest string that contains two or more strings as subsequences .

summary: NIST DADS defines shortest common superstring as: Find the shortest string that contains two or more strings as substrings .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shortestCommonSuperstring

label: shuffle sort
summary: NIST DADS defines shuffle sort as: A distribution sort algorithm that begins by removing the first 1/8 of the n items, sorting them (recursively), and putting them in an array. This creates n/8 buckets to which the remaining 7/8 of the items are distributed. Each bucket is then sorted, and the buckets are concatenated.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: shuffleSort

label: sibling
summary: NIST DADS defines sibling as: A node in a tree that has the same parent as another node is its sibling.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sibling

label: sieve of Eratosthenes
summary: NIST DADS defines sieve of Eratosthenes as: An algorithm to find all prime numbers up to a certain N. Begin with an (unmarked) array of integers from 2 to N. The first unmarked integer, 2, is the first prime. Mark every multiple of this prime. Repeatedly take the next unmarked integer as the next prime and mark every multiple of the prime.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: sieve

label: sift up
summary: NIST DADS defines sift up as: Restoring the heap property by swapping a node with its parent , and repeating the process on the parent until the root is reached or the heap property is satisfied.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: siftup

label: signature
summary: NIST DADS defines signature as: The types or domains , and order, in some representations, of inputs to and outputs from a function .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: signature

summary: NIST DADS defines simple uniform hashing as: The assumption or goal that items are equally likely to hash to any value.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simpleUniformHashing

summary: NIST DADS defines simple merge as: Merge n sorted streams into one output stream. All the stream heads are compared, and the head with the least key is removed and written to the output. This is repeated until all streams are empty.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplemerge

label: simple path
summary: NIST DADS defines simple path as: A path that repeats no vertex , except that the first and last may be the same vertex.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplepath

label: simplex
summary: NIST DADS defines simplex as: The simplest N-dimensional polytope . The generalization of a triangle (2D) or tetrahedron (3D).

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simplex

label: simulated annealing
summary: NIST DADS defines simulated annealing as: A technique to find a good solution to an optimization problem by trying random variations of the current solution. A worse variation is accepted as the new solution with a probability that decreases as the computation proceeds. The slower the cooling schedule , or rate of decrease, the more likely the algorithm is to find an optimal or near- optimal solution .

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simulatedAnnealing

label: simulation theorem
summary: NIST DADS defines simulation theorem as: One kind of computation can be simulated by another kind within stated complexity bounds. Most known containment or equality relationships between complexity classes were proved this way.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: simulatnthrm

summary: NIST DADS defines single-destination shortest-path problem as: Find the shortest path from each vertex in a weighted, directed graph to a specific destination vertex.

summary: NIST DADS defines single-source shortest-path problem as: Find the shortest paths from a specific source vertex to every other vertex in a weighted, directed graph . Dijkstra's algorithm solves this if all weights are nonnegative. The Bellman-Ford algorithm handles any weights.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleSourceShortestPath

label: single program multiple data
summary: NIST DADS defines single program multiple data as: The dominant style of parallel programming, where all processors use the same program, though each has its own data. Also known as SPMD.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singleprogrm

label: singularity analysis
summary: NIST DADS defines singularity analysis as: A complex asymptotic technique for determining the asymptotics of certain algebraic functions.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: singularity

summary: NIST DADS defines sink as: A vertex of a directed graph with no outgoing edges . More formally, a vertex with with out-degree 0.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skdtree

summary: NIST DADS defines skew symmetry as: The property that the flow is the same amount, but reversed direction, starting from either vertex of every edge of a flow network . More formally, for an edge e=(v,w), f(v,w) = -f(w,v), where f(a,b) is the flow from a to b.

summary: NIST DADS defines skip list as: A randomized variant of an ordered linked list with additional, parallel lists. Parallel lists at higher levels skip geometrically more items. Searching begins at the highest level, to quickly get to the right part of the list, then uses progressively lower level lists. sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: skiplist

summary: NIST DADS defines Smith algorithm as: A string matching algorithm which computes the shift value for both the rightmost character of the window and the character preceding it, then uses the maximum of the two values.

summary: NIST DADS defines Smith-Waterman algorithm as: A means of searching protein databases to find those with the best alignment.

summary: NIST DADS defines smoothsort as: A variant of heapsort that takes advantage of a partially ordered table. Performance is O(n) when input is sorted and O(n log n) performance for worst case .

summary: NIST DADS defines solvable as: A computational problem that can be solved by a Turing machine . The problem may have a nonbinary output.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: soundex

summary: NIST DADS defines source as: (1) A vertex of a directed graph with no incoming edges . More formally, a vertex with in-degree 0. (2) The vertex from which an edge of a directed graph leaves.

sources.title: NIST Dictionary of Algorithms and Data Structures: source

summary: NIST DADS defines space ordering method as: A mapping from a discrete k-dimensional space into a linear order.

summary: NIST DADS defines sparsification as: Technique for designing dynamic graph algorithms , which when applicable transform a time bound of T(n,m) onto O(T(n,n)), where m is the number of edges and n is the number of vertices of the given graph.

summary: NIST DADS defines sparsity as: Instances of the longest common subsequence problem in which the number of matches is small compared to the product of the lengths of the input strings.

summary: NIST DADS defines spatial access method as: A data structure to search for lines, polygons, etc. Also known as SAM.

summary: NIST DADS defines star encoding as: Using a fixed dictionary , encode words in text with strings having many repeated characters, typically an asterisk or "star" (*).

summary: NIST DADS defines star-shaped polygon as: A polygon P in which there exists an interior point p such that all the boundary points of P are visible from p.

summary: NIST DADS defines start state as: An initial state or condition of a finite state machine or Turing machine . Informally, how the memory is initially set.

summary: NIST DADS defines state as: The condition of a finite state machine or Turing machine at a certain time. Informally, the content of memory.

summary: NIST DADS defines Steiner vertex as: A point that is not part of the input set of points, for instance, a point computed to construct a Steiner tree .

label: Zhu-Takaoka
summary: NIST DADS defines Zhu-Takaoka as: A string matching algorithm that is a variant of the Boyer-Moore algorithm. It uses two consecutive text characters to compute the bad character shift. It is faster when the alphabet or pattern is small, but the skip table grows quickly, slowing the pre-processing phase.

label: zipper
summary: NIST DADS defines zipper as: A data structure equivalent to a binary tree that is "opened" so that some node is accessible. It consists of a pair: the current node, along with information to reconstruct the tree. Reconstruction information is called the path or context. A move-to-left-child operation returns the left subtree, along with a new path, which has (i) a Left value, (ii) the current node, (iii) the right subtree, and (iv) any previous path. A similar operation moves to the right child. A move-up operation returns a tree rebuilt from the path information and the current node, along with the previous path.

label: ZPP
summary: NIST DADS defines ZPP as: The class of languages for which a membership computation by a probabilistic Turing machine halts in polynomial time with no false acceptances or rejections, but randomly some "I don't know" answers. "ZPP" means " Z ero error P robability in P olynomial" time. Formal Definition: For a language, S, there exists a probabilistic Turing machine , M, that halts in polynomial time . M (correctly) accepts or rejects the string or, randomly, halts in an "I don't know" state.
